VIDEO.title: The Woman Wasn't Grabbing Jesus' Cloak, She Wanted THIS! (Matthew 9:18-38)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 9:18-38: a synagogue official's daughter raised, a woman healed when she touches the fringe of Jesus' garment, two blind men and a mute man healed, the Pharisees' accusation, and Jesus' compassion for crowds 'like sheep without a shepherd.' Mark 5:21-43 and Luke 8:40-56 give more detail; Mark and Luke name the official Jairus.

Matthew highlights faith: the official believes Jesus can raise his daughter, the woman reaches for His garment, and the blind men cry out. 'According to your faith' (9:29) means 'because you believe,' not 'in proportion to how much you believe.'

After the sermon (chapters 5-7), Jesus teaches, works miracles and walks out His own teaching at once. Like a good rabbi who taught from what was in view, He uses each miracle as a lesson about who He is. Raising the dead fits Isaiah 26:19, and later Jesus points John to His deeds (11:5).

The woman takes hold of the fringe: the video proposes one of the tassels (tzitzit) commanded in Numbers 15 and Deuteronomy 22. Malachi 4:2 promises the sun of righteousness 'with healing in its wings,' and the Hebrew kanaph means both wing and the corner of a garment. The video's reading: she was confessing Jesus as Messiah, and He praised her faith.

Seeing the crowds, Jesus is moved with compassion: they are like sheep without a shepherd. That points to Ezekiel 34, where God indicts Israel's shepherds, promises to seek His sheep Himself, and sets 'My servant David' over them. Israel is also God's vineyard (Isaiah 5). Jesus is the Good Shepherd come to rescue His flock and reap His harvest.

The lesson: Jesus' disciples must share His deep compassion and concern for the spiritual care of the harassed and helpless, expressed especially in how they pray. Is praying for the lost part of your prayer life?
QUOTES: The miracles that Jesus performed were opportunities for Jesus to teach.
Pay attention to the things that are odd in the Bible. They're odd for a reason.
She knew exactly where to grab him.
The Bible is a coloring book, but it's just all the color has been drained out of it.
Jesus wants his disciples to share his deep compassion and concern for the spiritual care of the harassed and the helpless.

method.p: The teacher's tip: these accounts get more detail in Mark 5:21-43, Luke 8:40-56 and Luke 11:14-15. And as you read anywhere in Scripture, pay attention to the things that are odd: they are odd for a reason.

LSB_QUOTES.text: for she was saying to herself, “If I only touch His garment, I will be saved from this.”
But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings
And seeing the crowds, He felt compassion for them, because they were distressed and downcast like sheep without a shepherd.

SIGNS.title: Come and lay Your hand on her

src.text: While He was saying these things to them, behold, a synagogue official came and was bowing down before Him, and said, “My daughter has just died; but come and lay Your hand on her, and she will live.”

lines.text: Matthew highlights faith in each scene. The official believes Jesus can bring his daughter back from death. Mark and Luke name him Jairus.
A synagogue official arranged services and readings. Turning to Jesus would have cost him standing with some colleagues.

src.text: And when He entered the house, the blind men came up to Him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to Him, “Yes, Lord.” Then He touched their eyes, saying, “It shall be done to you according to your faith.”

lines.text: Jesus does not answer them on the road; He waits until they come to Him in the house. 'According to your faith' is not about the quality or quantity of faith: it means 'because of the faith you have.'
Strangely, He tells them, 'See that no one knows about this!' (9:30), yet He does not stop the news of His other miracles. The teacher leaves it as something to notice.
'Son of David' is a royal, messianic title (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Crowds asked it again in 12:23, and the Pharisees answered with the same accusation as in 9:34.

src.text: And after the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke; and the crowds marveled, saying, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.” But the Pharisees were saying, “He casts out the demons by the ruler of the demons.”

lines.text: In the first century 'mute' could mean someone who could not speak, or someone who could neither speak nor hear.
The Greek kōphos covers both meanings: 'mute' here, 'deaf' in 11:5.

left.text: Your dead will live; / Their corpses will rise. / You who dwell in the dust, awake and shout for joy,

right.text: the blind receive sight and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.

lines.text: A good rabbi never taught in the abstract; he pointed to what was in view. Jesus uses each miracle to teach about Himself: forgiving the paralytic (9:2-6), and now raising the dead, which Isaiah's song of salvation looked for.
When John's disciples later ask, 'Are You the One who is to come?' (11:3), Jesus answers by pointing to these very deeds.
Jesus said the girl was 'asleep' (9:24). Jesus uses the same picture for Lazarus (John 11:11-14), and Paul for believers who have died (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14).

FRINGE.title: If I only touch His garment

src.text: And behold, a woman who had been suffering from a hemorrhage for twelve years, came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His garment; for she was saying to herself, “If I only touch His garment, I will be saved from this.” But Jesus turning and seeing her said, “Daughter, take courage; your faith has saved you.” At once the woman was saved from her hemorrhage.

lines.text: She did not reach for any spot. She grabbed the fringe of His garment, likely one of His tassels; she may even have pulled one loose, which helps explain how Jesus felt it.

Under the Law her condition made her unclean, as a corpse did for anyone who touched it (Leviticus 15:25; Numbers 19:11). Contact made a person unclean for a time; the Law did not forbid it. Here power flows the other way: she is made well.

src.text: Speak to the sons of Israel, and tell them that they shall make for themselves tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and that they shall put on the tassel of each corner a cord of blue. And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, so as to do them and not follow after your own heart and your own eyes,

right.text: You shall make yourself tassels on the four corners of your garment with which you cover yourself.

lines.text: Jewish men wore tassels on the four corners of the outer garment, to remember the Lord's commandments and not follow their own heart and eyes, as in the first sin in the garden.
Jesus later says the scribes and Pharisees 'lengthen the tassels of their garments' to be noticed (23:5). In 14:36 the sick at Gennesaret beg to touch just the fringe of His garment.

FRINGE.kicker: Malachi 4 · the last page before Matthew
FRINGE.title: Healing in its wings

src.text: But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings; and you will go forth and skip about like calves from the stall.

lines.text: The Hebrew for 'wings' (kanaph) is the same word used for the 'corners' that carry the tassels in Numbers 15:38 and Deuteronomy 22:12. The video reads 'the sun of righteousness' as the Messiah: He will bring healing in the fringe of His garment.
So when the woman grabbed Jesus' tassel, the video says, she was proclaiming that He was the long-awaited Messiah. Jesus knew it, and praised her faith: another teachable moment.
Malachi 4:5 promises Elijah before the day of Yahweh; Matthew 11:14 and 17:12 apply it to John the Baptist.

src.text: And Jesus was going through all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease and every kind of sickness. And seeing the crowds, He felt compassion for them, because they were distressed and downcast like sheep without a shepherd.

lines.text: Verse 35 nearly repeats 4:23. The teacher asks why Matthew repeats it, and leaves it for you to work out.
'Felt compassion' is a gut-level word. In Matthew's narrative it is always Jesus who feels it (14:14; 15:32; 20:34).
Moses prayed that Israel would not be 'like sheep which have no shepherd' (Numbers 27:17); Micaiah saw Israel scattered that way (1 Kings 22:17).

left.text: Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and say to those shepherds, ‘Thus says Lord Yahweh, “Woe, shepherds of Israel who have been shepherding themselves! Should not the shepherds shepherd the flock?

right.text: For thus says Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I Myself will seek My sheep and care for them.

lines.text: Read the whole chapter: it is a serious indictment of Israel's leaders. They fed themselves, not the flock (34:5-6, 10). So the Lord promises to be their shepherd Himself.
He also promises 'one shepherd, My servant David' (34:23), written centuries after David died: a pointer to the coming Messiah. Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd (John 10:11).

SHEPHERD.title: Pray to the Lord of the harvest

src.text: Then He said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into His harvest.”

lines.text: The odd part: instead of 'so go and reap it,' Jesus says pray. The harvest already belongs to the Lord. In chapter 10 He will send workers; for now He teaches them to pray earnestly.
God's people are pictured as sheep and as a vineyard (Isaiah 5:4, 7). Jesus takes up both pictures: now is the time to shepherd His people and reap His harvest.
The teacher thinks more than the Twelve heard this: Luke 10 has seventy more sent out, with the same words about the harvest.

TERMS.def: Hebrew for the tassels on the four corners of a garment (Numbers 15:38); the captions spell it 'tit.'
Greek kraspedon: the edge or tassel of a garment (9:20; 14:36; 23:5).
Hebrew 'wing'; also the corner or edge of a garment.
Malachi's picture of the day of Yahweh rising with healing (Malachi 4:2). The captions say 'son.'
A royal, messianic title for the promised heir of David.
Hebrew for disciples or students of a rabbi (singular talmid).
The Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings. Jesus saw the crowds 'through the lens of Tanakh.'
Ritually impure under the Law; it barred worship for a time, and could pass by touch (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19).
God as owner of the harvest; He sends the workers.

WORDS.gloss: Edge, fringe, tassel of a garment. Look up: BDAG, κράσπεδον.
To feel compassion, be moved in the inner parts. Look up: BDAG, σπλαγχνίζομαι.
Wing; corner or edge of a garment. Look up: BDB or HALOT, כָּנָף.

BACKGROUND.p: Numbers 15 and Deuteronomy 22 command tassels on the four corners of the outer garment, with a cord of blue. Jews still wear tzitzit on a prayer shawl or an undergarment.

Families hired flute-players and wailing women for funerals. The Mishnah records Rabbi Judah's rule: 'even the poorest man in Israel must provide no less than two flutes and one lamenting woman' (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4).

A flow of blood made a woman unclean, and touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Leviticus 15:25; Numbers 19:11). Uncleanness barred people from the temple and holy food until cleansing, but touching was not a sin.
Prophets called Israel's kings, priests and leaders 'shepherds.' Ezekiel 34 condemns them for feeding themselves, and promises God's own shepherding through David's heir.

WITNESSES.text: She was ashamed on account of her affliction, accounting herself to be unclean.

WITNESSES.text: Because though they were but twelve, He made them many from that time forward, not by adding to their number, but by giving them power.

DEBATES.p: The video: she grabbed a tassel because Malachi 4:2 promised healing in the Messiah's 'wings.' Others: the fringe was simply the edge she could reach from behind in a crowd. Matthew does not say; in 14:36 many others touch the fringe too.

DEBATES.h: Why tell the blind men to keep quiet?
DEBATES.p: Perhaps to avoid stirring up political hopes tied to 'Son of David,' or to keep crowds from hindering His work. Mark shows this pattern often. The teacher simply flags it as odd.
Chrysostom: the Twelve, made 'many' by power. The video: a wider circle of disciples, as in Luke 10's seventy. Both agree the first step is prayer.
Jesus praises faith here, yet He also heals people who show none (8:28-34). 'According to your faith' is not a formula for measuring faith.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Caption names and references: 'Gyrus' is Jairus, named in Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 (Matthew calls him a synagogue official in the LSB); 'Matthew 5... verse 30' is Mark 5:30; and Malachi's figure is the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2), not 'son.'

In Matthew the woman touches Jesus; He takes the girl by the hand (9:25) and touches the blind men's eyes (9:29). The Law did not forbid touching what was unclean; contact made a person unclean for a time (Leviticus 15:25-27; Numbers 19:11).
In Matthew's narrative only Jesus 'feels compassion,' but in His parables He uses the same verb for the master (18:27), the Samaritan (Luke 10:33) and the father of the lost son (Luke 15:20).
Malachi does not mention the Messiah's garment, and reading the woman's touch as a confession is the video's interpretation. The Gospels do not say why she chose the fringe.
Luke 10:1 reads 'seventy' in the LSB; some manuscripts read seventy-two. The video's 'Isaiah 5:4' fits the worthless grapes; the bloodshed and cry are in 5:7.

QUESTIONS: The official, the woman and the blind men each showed faith differently. Which one is most like you?
What 'odd' detail in this passage stood out to you, and what might it be teaching?
How does knowing Numbers 15 and Malachi 4 change how you picture the woman reaching for the fringe?
Jesus saw the crowds 'through the lens of Tanakh.' What would it look like for you to see people that way?
Who around you is 'distressed and downcast'? Name them before God this week.
Is praying for the lost an active part of your prayer, alone and with others?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: the disciples of Jesus must share His deep compassion and concern for the spiritual care of the harassed and the helpless. That compassion shows in their interactions with people, but especially in how they pray. When the crowds came, Jesus did not just see a crowd; He saw Ezekiel 34, sheep without a shepherd, and was moved at the gut level. Before He sends anyone out, He tells them to pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest. For the prayer warriors that comes easily; for the doers who want to fix things now, it is a real challenge. If Jesus wants His disciples to pray for the lost, is that what you are doing, alone and with your brothers and sisters? Think about how this applies to your life so that you can do something about it.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): write down three people who seem 'distressed and downcast like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36). Pray Matthew 9:38 for them by name each day this week, and ask the Lord of the harvest whether you are one of the workers He wants to send.

   (video) Matthew highlights faith in each scene. The official believes Jesus can bring his daughter back from death. Mark and Luke name him Jairus. (Mark 5:22-23; Luke 8:41-42)
   [Background] A synagogue official arranged services and readings. Turning to Jesus would have cost him standing with some colleagues.
2. Two blind men · Matthew 9:27-31: According to your faith
   Son of David Matthew 9:28-29: "And when He entered the house, the blind men came up to Him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to Him, “Yes, Lord.” Then He touched their eyes, saying, “It shall be done to you according to your faith.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:28-29
   (video) Jesus does not answer them on the road; He waits until they come to Him in the house. 'According to your faith' is not about the quality or quantity of faith: it means 'because of the faith you have.'
   (video) Strangely, He tells them, 'See that no one knows about this!' (9:30), yet He does not stop the news of His other miracles. The teacher leaves it as something to notice.
   [Background] 'Son of David' is a royal, messianic title (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Crowds asked it again in 12:23, and the Pharisees answered with the same accusation as in 9:34. (2 Samuel 7:12-16; Matthew 12:23-24)
3. A mute man · Matthew 9:32-34: Nothing like this in Israel
   Split Matthew 9:33-34: "And after the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke; and the crowds marveled, saying, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.” But the Pharisees were saying, “He casts out the demons by the ruler of the demons.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:33-34
   (video) In the first century 'mute' could mean someone who could not speak, or someone who could neither speak nor hear.
   [Background] The Greek kōphos covers both meanings: 'mute' here, 'deaf' in 11:5.
4. Lessons in the miracles · Isaiah 26:19: Your dead will live
   Isaiah (Isaiah 26:19, LSB): "Your dead will live; / Their corpses will rise. / You who dwell in the dust, awake and shout for joy,"
   Jesus (Matthew 11:5, LSB): "the blind receive sight and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them."
   (video) A good rabbi never taught in the abstract; he pointed to what was in view. Jesus uses each miracle to teach about Himself: forgiving the paralytic (9:2-6), and now raising the dead, which Isaiah's song of salvation looked for.
   (video) When John's disciples later ask, 'Are You the One who is to come?' (11:3), Jesus answers by pointing to these very deeds. (Matthew 11:2-6)
   [Background] Jesus said the girl was 'asleep' (9:24). Jesus uses the same picture for Lazarus (John 11:11-14), and Paul for believers who have died (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14).

## The fringe of His garment
1. The woman · Matthew 9:20-22: If I only touch His garment
   Fringe Matthew 9:20-22: "And behold, a woman who had been suffering from a hemorrhage for twelve years, came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His garment; for she was saying to herself, “If I only touch His garment, I will be saved from this.” But Jesus turning and seeing her said, “Daughter, take courage; your faith has saved you.” At once the woman was saved from her hemorrhage." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:20-22
   (video) She did not reach for any spot. She grabbed the fringe of His garment, likely one of His tassels; she may even have pulled one loose, which helps explain how Jesus felt it. (Mark 5:30; Luke 8:46)
   [Background] Under the Law her condition made her unclean, as a corpse did for anyone who touched it (Leviticus 15:25; Numbers 19:11). Contact made a person unclean for a time; the Law did not forbid it. Here power flows the other way: she is made well. (Leviticus 15:25-27; Numbers 19:11)
2. Tassels · Numbers 15:38-39: Tassels to remember
   Moses (Deuteronomy 22:12, LSB): "You shall make yourself tassels on the four corners of your garment with which you cover yourself."
   Tzitzit Numbers 15:38-39: "Speak to the sons of Israel, and tell them that they shall make for themselves tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and that they shall put on the tassel of each corner a cord of blue. And it shall be a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, so as to do them and not follow after your own heart and your own eyes," https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Numbers+15:38-39
   (video) Jewish men wore tassels on the four corners of the outer garment, to remember the Lord's commandments and not follow their own heart and eyes, as in the first sin in the garden. (Genesis 3:6)
   [Background] Jesus later says the scribes and Pharisees 'lengthen the tassels of their garments' to be noticed (23:5). In 14:36 the sick at Gennesaret beg to touch just the fringe of His garment. (Matthew 23:5; Matthew 14:36)
3. Malachi 4 · the last page before Matthew: Healing in its wings
   Kanaph Malachi 4:2: "But for you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings; and you will go forth and skip about like calves from the stall." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Malachi+4:2
   (video) The Hebrew for 'wings' (kanaph) is the same word used for the 'corners' that carry the tassels in Numbers 15:38 and Deuteronomy 22:12. The video reads 'the sun of righteousness' as the Messiah: He will bring healing in the fringe of His garment.
   (video) So when the woman grabbed Jesus' tassel, the video says, she was proclaiming that He was the long-awaited Messiah. Jesus knew it, and praised her faith: another teachable moment.
   [Background] Malachi 4:5 promises Elijah before the day of Yahweh; Matthew 11:14 and 17:12 apply it to John the Baptist. (Malachi 4:5; Matthew 11:14)

## Sheep without a shepherd
1. Compassion · Matthew 9:35-36: Sheep without a shepherd
   Compassion Matthew 9:35-36: "And Jesus was going through all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease and every kind of sickness. And seeing the crowds, He felt compassion for them, because they were distressed and downcast like sheep without a shepherd." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:35-36
   (video) Verse 35 nearly repeats 4:23. The teacher asks why Matthew repeats it, and leaves it for you to work out. (Matthew 4:23)
   (video) 'Felt compassion' is a gut-level word. In Matthew's narrative it is always Jesus who feels it (14:14; 15:32; 20:34). (Matthew 14:14; Matthew 15:32; Matthew 20:34)
   [Background] Moses prayed that Israel would not be 'like sheep which have no shepherd' (Numbers 27:17); Micaiah saw Israel scattered that way (1 Kings 22:17). (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17)
2. Ezekiel 34: Woe, shepherds of Israel
   Ezekiel (Ezekiel 34:2, LSB): "Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy and say to those shepherds, ‘Thus says Lord Yahweh, “Woe, shepherds of Israel who have been shepherding themselves! Should not the shepherds shepherd the flock?"
   God's promise (Ezekiel 34:11, LSB): "For thus says Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I Myself will seek My sheep and care for them."
   (video) Read the whole chapter: it is a serious indictment of Israel's leaders. They fed themselves, not the flock (34:5-6, 10). So the Lord promises to be their shepherd Himself. (Ezekiel 34:5-10)
   (video) He also promises 'one shepherd, My servant David' (34:23), written centuries after David died: a pointer to the coming Messiah. Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd (John 10:11). (Ezekiel 34:23; John 10:11)
3. The harvest · Matthew 9:37-38: Pray to the Lord of the harvest
   Pray Matthew 9:37-38: "Then He said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into His harvest.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+9:37-38
   (video) The odd part: instead of 'so go and reap it,' Jesus says pray. The harvest already belongs to the Lord. In chapter 10 He will send workers; for now He teaches them to pray earnestly.
   (video) God's people are pictured as sheep and as a vineyard (Isaiah 5:4, 7). Jesus takes up both pictures: now is the time to shepherd His people and reap His harvest. (Isaiah 5:1-7)
   (video) The teacher thinks more than the Twelve heard this: Luke 10 has seventy more sent out, with the same words about the harvest. (Luke 10:1-2)

## Key people
- Jesus: Raises the dead, heals, and uses each miracle to teach who He is; moved with compassion for shepherdless crowds. [Background] This is the third and last set of three miracles in chapters 8-9.
- The synagogue official (Jairus): Shows his faith: 'lay Your hand on her, and she will live.' [Background] Mark and Luke name him Jairus; at first his daughter was dying (Mark 5:23).
- The woman with a hemorrhage: Ill for twelve years; grabs the fringe of His garment, and Jesus praises her faith. [Background] Mark adds that she had spent all she had on doctors and only grew worse (Mark 5:26).
- The official's daughter: Raised from death; Jesus says she is asleep. [Background] Luke says she was about twelve (Luke 8:42).
- Flute-players and mourners: The crowd laughs at Jesus. [Background] Hired mourning was expected even of the poor (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4).
- Two blind men: Cry 'Have mercy on us, Son of David!' and are healed according to their faith. [Background] A similar pair appears near Jericho in 20:29-34.
- The mute man: Speaks after the demon is cast out. [Background] Luke 11:14-15 tells a similar healing with the same accusation.
- The Pharisees: Say He casts out demons by the ruler of the demons. [Background] The charge returns in 12:24 with the name Beelzebul.

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Jesus' 'own city' (9:1), likely the setting of these miracles; it had a synagogue (Mark 1:21).
- Gennesaret: Where the sick later begged to touch the fringe of His garment (14:34-36).
- Chorazin: One of the 'cities and villages' (9:35) that saw His miracles (11:21).
- Bethsaida: Another town that saw His works (11:21).
- Magdala: A fishing town on the west shore.

## Key terms
- Tzitzit: Hebrew for the tassels on the four corners of a garment (Numbers 15:38); the captions spell it 'tit.'
- Fringe: Greek kraspedon: the edge or tassel of a garment (9:20; 14:36; 23:5). [Background]
- Kanaph: Hebrew 'wing'; also the corner or edge of a garment.
- Sun of righteousness: Malachi's picture of the day of Yahweh rising with healing (Malachi 4:2). The captions say 'son.'
- Son of David: A royal, messianic title for the promised heir of David.
- Talmidim: Hebrew for disciples or students of a rabbi (singular talmid).
- Tanakh: The Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets and Writings. Jesus saw the crowds 'through the lens of Tanakh.'
- Unclean: Ritually impure under the Law; it barred worship for a time, and could pass by touch (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19). [Background]
- Lord of the harvest: God as owner of the harvest; He sends the workers.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Tassels on the corners: Numbers 15 and Deuteronomy 22 command tassels on the four corners of the outer garment, with a cord of blue. Jews still wear tzitzit on a prayer shawl or an undergarment.
- Mourning with flutes: Families hired flute-players and wailing women for funerals. The Mishnah records Rabbi Judah's rule: 'even the poorest man in Israel must provide no less than two flutes and one lamenting woman' (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4).
- Clean and unclean: A flow of blood made a woman unclean, and touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Leviticus 15:25; Numbers 19:11). Uncleanness barred people from the temple and holy food until cleansing, but touching was not a sin.
- Shepherds of Israel: Prophets called Israel's kings, priests and leaders 'shepherds.' Ezekiel 34 condemns them for feeding themselves, and promises God's own shepherding through David's heir.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Why the fringe? The video: she grabbed a tassel because Malachi 4:2 promised healing in the Messiah's 'wings.' Others: the fringe was simply the edge she could reach from behind in a crowd. Matthew does not say; in 14:36 many others touch the fringe too.
- Why tell the blind men to keep quiet? Perhaps to avoid stirring up political hopes tied to 'Son of David,' or to keep crowds from hindering His work. Mark shows this pattern often. The teacher simply flags it as odd.
- Who are the workers? Chrysostom: the Twelve, made 'many' by power. The video: a wider circle of disciples, as in Luke 10's seventy. Both agree the first step is prayer.
- Faith and healing Jesus praises faith here, yet He also heals people who show none (8:28-34). 'According to your faith' is not a formula for measuring faith.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Caption names and references: 'Gyrus' is Jairus, named in Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 (Matthew calls him a synagogue official in the LSB); 'Matthew 5... verse 30' is Mark 5:30; and Malachi's figure is the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2), not 'son.'
- In Matthew the woman touches Jesus; He takes the girl by the hand (9:25) and touches the blind men's eyes (9:29). The Law did not forbid touching what was unclean; contact made a person unclean for a time (Leviticus 15:25-27; Numbers 19:11).
- In Matthew's narrative only Jesus 'feels compassion,' but in His parables He uses the same verb for the master (18:27), the Samaritan (Luke 10:33) and the father of the lost son (Luke 15:20).
- Malachi does not mention the Messiah's garment, and reading the woman's touch as a confession is the video's interpretation. The Gospels do not say why she chose the fringe.
- Luke 10:1 reads 'seventy' in the LSB; some manuscripts read seventy-two. The video's 'Isaiah 5:4' fits the worthless grapes; the bloodshed and cry are in 5:7.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. The official, the woman and the blind men each showed faith differently. Which one is most like you?
2. What 'odd' detail in this passage stood out to you, and what might it be teaching?
3. How does knowing Numbers 15 and Malachi 4 change how you picture the woman reaching for the fringe?
4. Jesus saw the crowds 'through the lens of Tanakh.' What would it look like for you to see people that way?
5. Who around you is 'distressed and downcast'? Name them before God this week.
6. Is praying for the lost an active part of your prayer, alone and with others?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: the disciples of Jesus must share His deep compassion and concern for the spiritual care of the harassed and the helpless. That compassion shows in their interactions with people, but especially in how they pray. When the crowds came, Jesus did not just see a crowd; He saw Ezekiel 34, sheep without a shepherd, and was moved at the gut level. Before He sends anyone out, He tells them to pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest. For the prayer warriors that comes easily; for the doers who want to fix things now, it is a real challenge. If Jesus wants His disciples to pray for the lost, is that what you are doing, alone and with your brothers and sisters? Think about how this applies to your life so that you can do something about it.
- Study note (added): write down three people who seem 'distressed and downcast like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36). Pray Matthew 9:38 for them by name each day this week, and ask the Lord of the harvest whether you are one of the workers He wants to send.
